title: Brahma's lotus and the dry leaf
hookLine: Brahma is born on a lotus, and Krishna says to live like its leaf
carry: offer the work, stay untouched like the lotus
tomorrow: a sage who loved only half of God. what happened to him?
last: A WALL BUILT FOR COMING HOME THROUGH.

cards: Before there's a world, there's only water, dark and still, and Vishnu asleep on it, lying on the coils of a great serpent. From his navel a stem rises, and at its top a lotus opens.
In the lotus sits Brahma, the creator, with four faces, looking every way and seeing nothing but water. Where did he come from?
In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, he climbs down inside the stem to find its root, searching for ages, and never reaches the bottom. So he comes back up, sits still on his flower, and turns inward.
Only then does he see the Lord he grew from. And only then does he begin to make the world, seated on a lotus.

teach.b: That flower is everywhere in Hindu art: padma, the lotus. Brahma sits on one, Lakshmi stands on one, the Goddess is so often enthroned on one. Why?
A lotus grows up out of mud and opens clean, and its leaf sheds water: drops roll right off, and nothing sticks. Krishna uses exactly that picture in the Bhagavad Gita.
One who does their work as an offering to the divine, letting go of clinging to it, isn't stained by wrong, he says, any more than a lotus leaf is wet by water. That's karma yoga, the way of action.
You don't run from the muddy pond of ordinary life.

teach.h: THE GITA: OFFER THE WORK, DON'T CLING.
teach.b: You stay in it, do the work, and offer it. Now step through the yantra's gate.
The straight lines end and curves take over: three circles, then a ring of sixteen petals, then a ring of eight. The Saundarya Lahari counts them.
The yantra seats its center on lotuses, the way an image of a god is set on a lotus seat.
And that's how the tradition pictures a holy life: rising out of the mud, untouched by it.

how: Many Hindus close a task or a meal with the words 'Krishnarpanam astu', offering it to Krishna; in Sri Vidya worship the lotus rings of the Sri Yantra are honored as layers of the Goddess's dwelling on the way to the center.

o: a garden design planted for a goddess's festival
a flower offering laid in rings around a temple floor
a lotus seat: the holy rising clean out of the mud

p: born on a lotus from Vishnu's navel
untouched by water, like offered work

s: in the Bhagavata, Brahma climbs down the lotus stem and finds its root
he searches for ages and never reaches it; he sees the Lord only when he sits still and turns inward.
in the Gita, Krishna compares one who offers their work to a lotus leaf on water
the water rolls off: clinging doesn't stick.
the Gita's lotus means leaving ordinary life behind
it means staying in the pond: doing the work and offering it.

games.q: a friend says she can't be spiritual until she quits her stressful job. what does Krishna's lotus picture say?
o: do the work as an offering, without clinging; the lotus leaf stays dry in the water.
leave the pond first; a lotus can only stay clean out of the water.
skip the work; the Gita says holiness is found only in sitting still.
games.why: in the Gita, one who offers their work and lets go of clinging stays untouched, like a lotus leaf on water. that's karma yoga.

practice: Join your palms in front of your heart. Think of one job waiting for you today, ordinary and a bit muddy: a call, a chore, a stack of boxes.
Many Hindus finish a task or a meal with two words: Krishnarpanam astu, let this be offered to Krishna. Say it softly for your one job, or, if you don't pray, simply: i offer this.
Then picture a lotus leaf on dark water, and the drops rolling off.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Yantra, one step in: its lotus rings, sixteen petals and then eight, a seat for the holy that rises clean out of the mud.

orig.note: Sanskrit padma, lotus: the yantra's rings of petals.

carryVoice: For the road: offer the work, stay untouched like the lotus. Brahma was born on one. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 3.8: Brahma appears on the lotus from Vishnu's navel, searches down the stem for its root, and sees the Lord only after turning inward
Bhagavad Gita 5.10: one who acts offering their work to Brahman, giving up attachment, is not stained by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water
Saundarya Lahari 11: the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled lotuses, three circles and three lines among the parts of the Goddess's dwelling
Krishnarpanam astu: words many Hindus say to offer a task or a meal to Krishna
